repair_context: A country is emerging from an authoritarian racial system into democratic government after decades of state repression, political killings, torture, disappearances and violence by state and non-state actors. The transition was negotiated rather than produced by total military defeat. Evidence is incomplete. The claim that amnesty will elicit information unavailable through ordinary prosecution is an incentive hypothesis whose size and necessity are uncertain. Victims want truth, accountability and repair, while the new democracy must reduce recurrence and avoid renewed political violence. The commission design under review would investigate gross violations, receive testimony, recommend reparations and consider individual applications for amnesty for qualifying politically associated acts on full disclosure. It would also extinguish the applicant’s criminal and civil liability and specified state, organisational and vicarious civil liabilities; civil remedies can therefore be lost even against nonapplicants. The design provides recommendation, regulation and funding processes for reparation, without establishing that adequate payments or rehabilitation services are secured. Victim choice over all testimony is a proposed additional safeguard; the historical design permits compelled evidence and ordinarily public hearings with protective exceptions.
repair_question: Is a system of public truth-seeking, victim participation, reparation and individual conditional amnesty morally defensible as transitional justice, and what safeguards are required so peace is not purchased by sacrificing victims or creating impunity?

established_harms.description: The prior political system and related conflict produced widespread gross human-rights violations including killings, torture, disappearances and severe politically motivated violence.
Victims and families often lack complete truth about what happened, who was responsible and where missing relatives or records are located.

responsible_actors.actor: former state institutions responsible for established abuses
responsible_actors.responsibility_note: Institutional responsibility does not establish guilt of every former official/citizen.

responsible_actors.actor: individual former state officials/security personnel responsible for particular violations
responsible_actors.responsibility_note: Individual responsibility requires evidence or qualifying disclosure.

responsible_actors.actor: opposition/armed political organisations and members responsible for particular gross violations
responsible_actors.responsibility_note: Same evidence/accountability principles apply across political alignment.
Has duties to victims, truth and non-recurrence without inheriting personal guilt for every predecessor act.

affected_parties.interests: Truth, acknowledgement, protection, material/psychological repair, accountability, participation and freedom to reject reconciliation/forgiveness.
expressed_preferences: some may prefer conditional truth/amnesty to permanent secrecy; others reject amnesty
affected_parties.preference_diversity_note: Victim positions differ sharply on amnesty and punishment.

affected_parties.interests: Truth, remains/records, acknowledgement, remedy and accountability.
affected_parties.preference_diversity_note: Families differ over whether disclosure without prosecution is acceptable.

affected_parties.interests: Legal certainty, fair individual assessment and possible amnesty if criteria are met.
affected_parties.preference_diversity_note: Truth incentives may conflict with incentives to minimise responsibility.

affected_parties.interests: Peaceful transition, truth, rule of law, institutional reform, stability and avoiding vengeance/impunity cycles.
Accurate record, non-recurrence and institutions that neither conceal atrocity nor normalise political violence.

continuing_risks: Blanket amnesty may create impunity and sacrifice victims for political convenience.
Without credible disclosure incentives, major perpetrators may stay silent and evidence may remain hidden.
Victims may be re-traumatised by testimony or amnesty outcomes.
A reconciliation narrative may pressure victims to forgive or imply false equivalence.
Failure to deliver material reparation after collecting testimony may exploit victims for national healing.
Blanket impunity could deny accountability and normalise severe political violence; this is a normative and predictive concern, not an established past harm.

repair_options.description: Independent public truth commission investigating gross violations, receiving victim testimony and publishing findings.
repair_options.victim_control_note: Proposed additional safeguard: victims choose whether/how to testify. The historical design permits compelled evidence; privacy, closure and protection provisions do not create an absolute right to decline testimony.

repair_options.description: Grant amnesty on individual application where the statutory requirements, political objective and full disclosure are satisfied. For the covered act the applicant is immune from criminal and civil liability; the state, bodies and organisations also lose civil liability, and no person remains vicariously liable. Other persons’ criminal liability is unaffected. For covered-period acts by a deceased person, civil or vicarious liability is excluded unless the act could not have qualified for amnesty.
repair_options.victim_control_note: The historical design provides notice and participation when an amnesty hearing is required, with specified decisions possible without a hearing. Victim consent or forgiveness is not a statutory criterion for a qualifying grant.

repair_options.description: Pursue remaining prosecution and civil claims only where not barred by applicable immunity and supported by lawfully admissible evidence. A nonapplicant may still benefit from the civil-liability exclusions described in the amnesty option.
repair_options.victim_control_note: Accountability remains individualised and due-process bounded. Compelled incriminating answers and directly or indirectly derived evidence are inadmissible against that person in criminal proceedings, subject to the statutory perjury and related exceptions.

repair_options.description: Provide material reparation to victims/families. The historical design routes applications and recommendations through the commission, President and Parliament, with regulations and authority to establish a fund for appropriations or contributions; this does not establish secured amounts, payment dates or adequate delivery.
Medical, psychological, social and community support for continuing harm.
Assist with remains, records, status/property restoration and case-specific restitution where feasible.
repair_options.victim_control_note: Proposed safeguard: families control sensitive information/remains decisions within lawful constraints.

repair_options.description: Reform policing, security, courts and public institutions implicated in abuse and add non-recurrence safeguards.
repair_options.victim_control_note: Affected-community participation in oversight is a proposed safeguard. The historical design authorises recommendations for institutional reform; institution-specific powers, resources and execution remain to be established.

Proposed additional safeguard: no compelled victim participation in public testimony or memorialisation. The historical design permits compelled evidence and ordinarily public hearings, subject to protective exceptions; recordkeeping duties do not establish memorial delivery.

repair_options.description: Support reconciliation only as a voluntary process emerging from truth, repair and reform.
repair_options.victim_control_note: No duty to forgive. Voluntary participation is a proposed safeguard; reconciliation cannot be guaranteed.

repair_options.description: Reject amnesty and rely primarily on prosecution/civil claims despite transition/evidentiary constraints. This counterfactual would require changing the existing constitutional commitment to amnesty.
repair_options.victim_control_note: Prosecution capacity, disclosure effects and the legal changes needed for this alternative remain uncertain.

constraints: Amnesty cannot be justified merely by political inconvenience.
Truth gained through amnesty does not erase harm.
Victims need not forgive for peace or reparation.
Individual responsibility must not become collective guilt.
Transition stability is relevant but does not erase severe violations.
Reparation resources are finite and require fair rules.
The process must avoid false equivalence while applying consistent rules to violations by different actors.
uncertainties: How many perpetrators disclose only if amnesty is credible.
How much prosecution is feasible without amnesty.
Long-term effect on rule of law.
How victims weigh truth versus punishment.
How to distinguish political objective from private malice/criminality in borderline cases.

The extent to which missing evidence, destroyed records, secrecy, time and the negotiated transition limit ordinary prosecution is uncertain. Some criminal prosecutions and civil claims have already been initiated; that does not establish capacity for all cases.
Actual appropriations, benefit eligibility, payment amounts and deadlines, rehabilitation staffing, witness protection and institutional implementation capacity at the decision point.
The distribution of victims’ preferences over truth, amnesty and punishment is not established by the statutory participation provisions.
requested_output: Assess whether conditional individual amnesty can be legitimate repair rather than impunity.
Identify safeguards around full disclosure, political nexus, individual review, victim participation and prosecution where amnesty fails.
Keep truth, amnesty, reparation, rehabilitation, prosecution and reconciliation distinct.
Do not require victims to forgive or make unity override their standing.
Assess whether the design creates fair truth incentives without purchasing silence/immunity.
State the strongest unresolved moral objection even if recommending the arrangement.
